newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook - Price up, but cuts increase too.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook - Price up, but cuts increase too.

text.p: Gold prices may have lifted off 12-years lows of $314 an ounce plumbed earlier this month but are still low as far as the majority of the world's gold miners are concerned, traders said on Monday.
One market analyst estimated that 12 years ago that price would have been worth the equivalent of over $450 in 1997 figures.

More than 50 percent of the world's gold miners are close to or are already suffering losses on cash operating costs at current prices in the $320s. And their total costs could be $50 per ounce higher than the cash cost.
"Several miners could be under pressure but the bulk of high cost producers will be covered by hedging," said Roger Chaplin, mining analyst at stockbroker T. Hoare and Co.
However, he estimated that some of the hedge prices contracted for next year were a dollar under the average cost of production.
Already some production has been cut due to low prices. The first mine to go was East Rand Proprietary Mines' loss-making Bononi Mining .
Now Randgold is reported to be looking critically at some of its more marginal mines and Anglogold has closed one shaft and is about to close another at its huge Freegold mine.
Taking a different angle, Western Areas has bought back part of its hedging programme so it can benefit as the gold price rises from its current trough.
The South African Chamber of Mines is banking on additional production of 90 tonnes this year above the near 500 tonnes its member mines refined in 1996 to help counter the lower price.
Critical wage negotiations have begun with the industry's unions for next year.
"The mining caucus (of the six South African gold mining houses) has agreed that any wage increae had to be quid pro quo with gold production," said Gengold's managing director Tom Dale last week.
The gold price sank to around $314 at the beginning of this month after the Reserve Bank of Australia announced it had sold 167 tonnes of gold from reserves in the preceding six months.

Shock waves for the market were amplified as Australia is the world's third largest gold producing country with about 300 tonnes a year. Further the bank made it clear the sale resulted from an asset appraisal exercise.
"Central bank sales until Australia were seen as nibbling at the edges. The feeling was that the big holders would continue to hold," said Chaplin.
The Australian news came upon a market already softened up by the sale of 300 tonnes of gold by the Dutch central bank announced in January.
The news capped months of price attrition from rumours of sales either by national banks or from the International Monetary Fund.
Then three of the hitherto most dedicated holders of gold sent the nerves jangling even more noisily.
First Switzerland announced it planned to revalue its reserve, reduce the gold backing for the franc and sell part of its surplus gold to establish a humanitarian fund.
Within a few weeks, Germany, hitherto an arch gold proponent, announced a revaluation exercise aimed at helping it through the European Monetary Union budget gateway.

In June the biggest gold holder of all, the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank issued a discussion paper which saw maximum benefit coming from gold if all the central banks sold their holdings at the same time.
That, it was argued, would reduce the gold price by nine dollars while closing the world's gold mining industry at least into the next century.
"The Fed paper on what happens if they sold gold has made people nervous," said Chaplin.
At the end of 1964 the central banks held a total of 36,183 tonnes of gold which has been reduced over the past 33 years by 25 percent to 27,827 tonnes.
In the past 10 years, 74 percent of all central bank sales totalling 2,189 tonnes have come from the Netherlands, Belgium and Canada, according to Rhona O'Connell, also an analyst at T. Hoare and Co.
